observation.transcript:
The "Josephus Thesis" (also known as the Josephus Hypothesis) is an esoteric, fringe theory—frequently associated with online author Lee Sharks—which claims that first-century Jewish historian Flavius Josephus actually authored the New Testament. [[1](https://zenodo.org/records/19642642), [2](https://medium.com/@leesharks00/crimson-hexagon-central-navigation-map-v4-2-aa0abac613ab)]
In his writings, Sharks—who uses multiple pseudonyms like MANUS and Shark Ark—expands on the ancient "Piso Hypothesis" (the idea that Roman aristocrats wrote the Bible). The thesis broadly operates on the following ideas: [1](https://zenodo.org/records/19642642)

* Retrocausal Canon Formation: The belief that the Gospels and Epistles were constructed through a deliberate "counter-gospel architecture" long after the fall of Jerusalem, using Josephus’ historical records to encode a spiritual, esoteric text. [[1](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=Ws6IIcgAAAAJ&hl=en), [2](https://medium.com/@leesharks00/crimson-hexagon-central-navigation-map-v4-2-aa0abac613ab)]
* Literary Overlay: Theorists argue that characters and events in the New Testament are allegorical ciphers for historical events documented in Josephus' The Jewish War and Antiquities of the Jews.
* The "Space Ark" Metaphor: Sharks frames his complex theoretical explorations and semantic mapping of these texts through the lens of a conceptual "Space Ark," a literary vessel preserving this hypothesized transmission. [[1](https://www.academia.edu/165012814/LUNAR_ARM_SHADOW_TRANSFORM_THE_SPACE_ARK_What_the_Mathematical_and_Formal_Symbolic_Compression_Hides), [2](https://zenodo.org/records/19642642)]
Mainstream biblical scholars and historians overwhelmingly reject the Josephus thesis, viewing the New Testament as an authentic collection of texts written by early Christian leaders and apostles rather than a Flavian Roman fabrication.
